people.about: Confucius's favourite disciple, poor, quiet and fond of learning, who died young. The Master's grief at his death is one of the few places the book shows him weeping.
The bold, impetuous disciple, quick to act and quick to object, often rebuked and plainly loved. He died in a political struggle in the state of Wei.
Eloquent and capable, a successful merchant and diplomat. He asks many of the book's questions and in its last pages defends his teacher against those who rank him higher than Confucius.

A younger disciple remembered for self-examination and filial piety. Legge calls him "the philosopher Tsang"; the title marks him as a teacher in his own right, and many scholars think his own students helped compile the book.
A disciple who speaks in Book I with the title of a master. Legge writes "the philosopher Yu", a different name from Zilu's personal name, which Legge also writes "Yu".
A disciple known for learning and the old texts, later a teacher at the court of Wei. Many sayings of Book XIX are his.
A younger disciple, ambitious and impressive in manner, who asks about official employment, about distinction and about how to be understood.
A capable administrator who served the powerful Ji family. Confucius praises his ability and, when he helps the family grow richer at the people's cost, disowns him.
A clever speaker whom Confucius rebukes more sharply than anyone: for sleeping in the daytime, and for arguing that three years of mourning are too long.
A disciple praised for virtue and for filial piety, who refuses office under the Ji family.
A disciple who drives the Master's carriage and asks plain questions about virtue and knowledge, and once about growing grain, which Confucius declines to teach.
A disciple known for learning and ritual, governor of the town of Wu-ch'ang, where Confucius hears the music of strings and smiles.
A disciple of humble birth whom Confucius thinks fit to rule, and who asks about perfect virtue and about government.
A disciple skilled in ceremony, who in the book's longest scene wishes only to serve as a minor assistant at the ancestral temple.
Head of the Ji family, the real power in the state of Lu in Confucius's last years. He asks about government, and the answers are among the book's sharpest.
The ruler of Lu in Confucius's old age, holding a title whose power had passed to the great families.
A statesman of Qi about a century before Confucius, who made his ruler leader of the states. The Analects judge him both ways: small in ritual, great in what he achieved.
